newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's Khatami treads warily in choosing ministers.
newsitem.headline: Iran's Khatami treads warily in choosing ministers.

text.p: Iran's new President Mohammad Khatami is moving carefully to gain approval for his cabinet choices from conservatives who dominate parliament, political analysts and diplomats based in Tehran said on Monday.

They said the moderate Shi'ite Moslem cleric was facing opposition from conservatives and hardliners particularly over his choices for sensitive ministries such as foreign affairs, intelligence (internal security) and culture.
"Khatami has to tread very carefully...he has to learn to walk before he can run. Nothing has been won yet even with the election victory," one Western diplomat said.

The Majlis, the 270-member parliament which holds its next session on Tuesday, is dominated by conservatives headed by speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri whom Khatami crushed at the polls on promises of social and economic reform.
Some newspapers said on Monday Khatami would present his list of cabinet ministers to parliament on Tuesday. Khatami, who has legally until next Monday to do so, has not confirmed this.

"There is every likelihood that the President will go to the Majlis tomorrow with his list for the cabinet...It is also clear that the president is under pressure to include some names from certain factions," Iran News daily reported.
Khatami has not publicly discussed his ministerial choices, although newspapers have speculated widely on the cabinet list.

The daily Hamshahri said Khatami had chosen conservative cleric and parliament deputy Qorbanali Dorri-Najafabadi as intelligence minister. If confirmed, the move would be an important concession by Khatami to his opponents.

The newspaper said Khatami was insisting on picking Iran's ambassador to the United Nations Kamal Kharrazi as foreign minister and vice-president Ataollah Mohajerani as culture minister, choices strongly opposed by conservatives.
Other press reports said Mohajerani, widely attacked for having advocated direct talks with the United States in 1990, was no longer a candidate.
Khatami's list also included Abdollah Nouri, a leader of a pro-Khatami group of radical clerics who have moderated their views in recent years, as interior minister, Hamshahri said.

The pro-Khatami newspaper said the 54-year-old cleric had also selected the outgoing energy minister Bijan Namdar Zanganeh as oil minister and Hossein Namazi as economy and finance minister, a post he had held in the 1980s.

Iranian newspapers, many of which are run by political factions, have carried fierce commentary in recent days on who should be in Khatami's cabinet and on the relative powers of the presidency and the parliament in deciding appointments.

"Khatami may well be a cultured, respected man but he will very much have to have all the skills of a fox to work round his opponents and deliver on his election pledges," said another foreign diplomat based in Tehran.

Newspapers said opposition by conservatives and entrenched revolutionaries had already forced Khatami to drop Tehran's reformist mayor Gholamhossein Karbaschi, a key backer, from even being proposed for full cabinet rank.
"Men like Karbaschi who carried out major changes in this city are just too hot to handle for some of those in parliament backed by the powerful merchants," the foreign diplomat said.

Analysts said compromise by Khatami on key cabinet positions could shape and even hamper any future attempts to push through change and breathe fresh life into the 18-year-old Islamic revolutionary state.
"The main offices of the cabinet may be out of his hands. Then there will be very little he can do as a president but bring limited changes in social affairs," said one analyst.

Khatami was elected on the back of Iran's large youth vote, women and its growing middle classes who saw in him a chance of introducing more social freedoms such as a relaxation of restrictive dress codes and legalising satellite dishes for foreign television programmes.
